prompt: Your site comes under an application-layer (L7) DDoS: 200,000 req/s of valid-looking `GET /search?q=<random>` requests spread approximately evenly across ~50,000 residential IPs. Normal traffic is 5,000 req/s and each search costs ~50 ms of database CPU time. Which defence plan is strongest?

options.text: Rely on autoscaling the search tier to absorb the traffic
options.explanation: Random queries defeat useful cache reuse and concentrate expensive work on the database. Scaling application servers alone does not remove that bottleneck and can increase the cost of the attack.
The prompt spreads the attack over many residential sources, so blocking a small set leaves most traffic intact.

options.text: Edge protection (CDN/WAF) with bot detection and challenges, rate limits per IP and per session, origin locked to the edge, and load shedding plus a cheaper degraded search
options.explanation: Correct. Layered defences: the edge filters and challenges bots before they reach you; rate limits cap each client; the origin can't be bypassed; and shedding protects the database while serving users a degraded but working search.

options.text: Switch search from GET to POST
options.explanation: Attackers can send POSTs just as easily. It changes nothing about request volume or cost, and makes legitimate caching harder.

workedExample: The requests look valid individually but create expensive aggregate work, and many sources defeat simple per-IP limits. Filter and challenge at the edge, rate limit identities as well as addresses, and authenticate the intended edge at the origin. Bound search concurrency and provide a cheap safe fallback. Challenges and caches have limits; monitor false positives and keep origin work within measured capacity.

link.title: AWS best practices for DDoS resiliency

prompt: Attackers send small UDP requests to exposed reflectors using the victim’s spoofed source address. The reflectors return much larger replies. Which explanation and defence are correct?

options.text: Only request sizes change; the victim receives no additional volume
options.explanation: The victim receives the larger reflected responses, so incoming traffic can greatly exceed the attackers’ request traffic.

options.text: Encrypting the victim’s database stops the reflected traffic
options.explanation: Storage encryption does not prevent a network link being flooded.

options.text: Large replies converge on the victim; remove exposed reflectors, filter spoofed sources and use upstream DDoS protection
options.explanation: Correct. Reflector capacity and network overhead limit real amplification; a local firewall alone cannot recover bandwidth already consumed upstream.

options.text: A firewall at the victim prevents its internet link from filling
options.explanation: Packets can saturate the link before the firewall discards them.

workedExample: The forged source address redirects replies to the victim. The response/request size imbalance amplifies traffic, but actual volume depends on reflector and network capacity. Disable unnecessary public UDP exposure, apply filtering of forged source addresses, and absorb/filter floods upstream of the constrained origin link.
